Ford is currently under investigation by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s Office of Defects Investigation for more than a million vehicles whose front airbags could cause serious burns. According to the Preliminary Evaluation documents filed with the ODI, the investigation covers an estimated 1,236,155 Ford Explorer SUVs built between the 2021 and 2026 model years.

The investigation documents explain that the ODI has received eight Vehicle Owner Questionnaires and four Early Warning Reporting “Death and Injury” reports that include allegations of burn injuries caused by the deployment of the seat-mounted side airbags. In each case, the injuries were limited to the driver, the front passenger, or both; the report didn’t detail any injuries to rear passengers or fatalities of any kind.

Sound familiar? Yeah, it looks like BYD is gunning for the Rolls-Royce Phantom’s spot as the ultimate luxury sedan.

Though closer in size to the Rolls-Royce Ghost , the Altior, which means “higher” in Latin, aims to offer an elevated passenger experience rooted in Chinese tradition. Wolfgang Egger, BYD’s design director, says the Altior was inspired by the “ding,” ancient bronze cauldrons that symbolize strength, dignity, and harmony. Even the air vents have cultural significance, featuring inlays of yellow Hetian jade, which is traditionally associated with wealth, prosperity, and authority. Actually racing in the rain had become as rare as spotting a dodo bird in the wild.

Saturday previewed both sides of the wet-weather coin. After a heavy downpour delayed Q1 by more than an hour, fans were treated to one of the season's best qualifying sessions. Wily veterans Fernando Alonso and Nico Hülkenberg dragged their subpar equipment into Q3. Car safety has come a long way since the days of yore. Ask the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS). The organization's crash testing standards have evolved significantly over 30+ years as more new vehicles keep getting better at protecting their occupants. By now, we're pretty familiar with the IIHS Top Safety Pick awards. However, just because your second-gen 2011 Hyundai Tucson has the Top Safety Pick under its belt doesn't mean it's as safe as the third-gen 2021 model, which also happens to be a Top Safety Pick winner.

Although the IIHS rates the small SUV highly , understand that it also keeps updating the award's eligibility criteria as the years go by. For example, headlights were not even part of the Top Safety Pick criteria in 2010, nor were vehicle-to-vehicle or pedestrian crash-prevention features. And Top Safety Pick+ wasn't even a thing before 2013. In fact, looking at the many generations of the small SUV, it's fair to conclude that fourth-generation Tucsons (2022-2026) appear to be the safest, according to the IIHS. Not only have certain fourth-generation Tucsons gone through the organization's slew of updated testing standards, but they have consistently been part of the IIHS Top Safety Pick+ category between 2022 and 2026, unlike the third or prior generation models.

For the past couple years, Flock Safety and its vast network of spy cameras have been all over the news, and for numerous reasons. Whether you've heard about them because of the staggering number of Flock cameras dotting US highways , because of the CEO calling Flock detractors terrorists, or the massive number of cops that keep getting arrested for illegally using automatic license plate readers (ALPRS) to stalk people , one thing's for sure: You've definitely seen news about this state-sponsored private surveillance network (and its similarly dubiously-intentioned competitors, like Axon ) for one reason or another. But you might be surprised to learn that you can trace a line back through history from modern surveillance tech like ALPRs back to the some of the first streetlights, which appeared in Paris in the late 1600s.

Like ALPRs, these public lights weren't well-loved by the public, especially by revolutionaries and the lower classes, who were particularly affected by the policing the lights enabled. The similarities don't end there, though. Just like people today love vandalizing Flock cameras and other ALPRs , the Parisians of the 17 th and 18 th centuries loved smashing the lanterns lighting up the city streets. Like today, such vandalism carried significant legal ramifications, but people still saw fit to express their discontent by destroying the lights, a behavior that only became more popular with the beginning of the French Revolution.

When it comes to fun-per-dollar, it's difficult to argue that these don't peg the needle squarely in the as-much-as-you-want zone. However, to keep costs low, manufacturers tend to skip most of the equipment and paperwork you would need for them to be legally plated and ridden on the street.

Most of these electric dirt bikes come fresh off the boat from China. You've heard of the big names, like Surron or Talaria, I'm sure. These days there are dozens of other manufacturers building (or white-label reselling) these machines for distribution through just about every online retailer you can think of.

Briefing: Equipping a sports car with a big and powerful engine is all well and good. But if the car in question is designed like a cinder block, then it's just wasting the engine's potential. As a car speeds up, the air resistance around it increases.

Equipping a sports car with a big and powerful engine is all well and good. But if the car in question is designed like a cinder block, then it's just wasting the engine's potential. As a car speeds up, the air resistance around it increases. And a car with a sleeker design can slip through the air with less resistance, thus granting it better performance. That, in a very basic nutshell, is why aerodynamics matter.

Now, drag coefficient (Cd) isn't the be-all and end-all when it comes to measuring a car's aerodynamics as a whole. Something like drag area, which combines that metric with frontal area measurements, provides a more complete picture. Nevertheless, drag coefficient scores still provide a solid impression as to just how slippery a car is — and such figures are more readily available from automakers, too.

Imagining a collage of objects of American culture, the mind conjures up images of things like sports stadiums, a drive-thru menu, the Wall Street Bull, the Hollywood sign, blue jeans, apple pie, and likely, some kind of car. Cars, our car dependency, and the American love for V8 engines are integral to our culture, and there are no cars to demonstrate this better than the pony car family. While very similar, there are some differences between a muscle car and a pony car.

To put it simply, the muscle car and the pony car are two sides of the same coin. The muscle car was bigger and purely focused on looking cool and going fast, with not much thought to anything else. The pony car took all that was fun about the muscle car, including the good looks and exciting performance, and made it all a bit easier to live with, often by being smaller than its muscle car counterparts. The Mustang started the pony car trend, but it wasn't the only one to do it. Since those early days in the 1960s, we've seen different takes from different manufacturers, including models like the Chevrolet Camaro, the Dodge Challenger, and even some from the hands of Carroll Shelby. Many of these models have stuck around to the modern day. The spirit of the pony car is old, but it is far from gone.

The Tesla Cybertruck is one of the most polarizing vehicles of our time, largely due to its unconventional silhouette and the lack of curves on its stainless steel body. Besides grabbing the attention of onlookers, owners have another thing to worry about that has to do with maintenance costs — the tires. Changing the rubber on your Tesla pickup truck requires a higher budget than your average full-size truck, and can exceed the $2,000 mark on flagship trims. Furthermore, the Cybertruck's tires might need to be replaced sooner than expected due to its immense weight and torque figures.

Of course this is not limited to Tesla, as the Rivian R1T suffers from similar issues. According to Tesla's manual, the entry-level Cybertruck with 18-inch wheels wears all-season Goodyear Wrangler Territory HT rubber (285/70R18). Stepping up to 20-inch wheels, you can either have all-season Pirelli Scorpion ATR tires (285/65R20), or the heavier-duty Goodyear Wrangler Territory R/T (LT285/65R20). The latter feature a bespoke sidewall design tailored for the wheel covers of the Cybertruck . Finally, owners in cold regions can opt for the 20-inch Goodyear Wrangler DuraTrac R/T.

Deer are a hazard drivers have to contend with. Sure, we could put some murder kitties in the forests, because more big cats in forests can reduce car crashes by roughly 75% . Or, we could install crossings to give creatures a safe path over big roads, like they did in California with the world's largest wildlife crossing . But short of that, accidents with deer will happen. State Farm reports that there were more than 1.6 million animal-related collisions between July 2025 and July 2026. It is a real concern.
